title: Dōgen's Points of Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō Zuimonki, the informal talks given at Kōshōji and recorded by Ejō, read here in Shohaku Okumura's translation, and follows four themes through it. Aspiration comes first, with a student of the Buddha who could not remember a single verse yet attained verification within one summer practice period. Impermanence follows through Norman's grief when his friend Alan Lew died on a morning jog, and through a visit with Edie Norton, now on hospice, to choose a name for a November Jukai. Generosity brings Eisai breaking up the copper meant for a Medicine Buddha's halo to feed a starving family. Nomon ends by linking that story to the man who slept under a table in the old downtown space and was nicknamed MUTA.

sentences.text: Hi everybody.
We're excited to focus most of our studies and teachings this year on Dogen.
We are always having Dogen somewhere in our minds.
I remember well that part of why Peter is even here is Chris's Dogen group invited him back to Red Cedar after some years away, and he has remained steady at that practice in Chris's group.
What is being read in Chris's group is called *Shobogenzo*, a collection of essays.
That Japanese term means something like "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye," but since everything Dogen is called *Shobogenzo*, it is a little bit confusing.
What I would like to share this morning is a text called *Dogen Shobogenzo Zuimonki*.
Zuimonki has three characters, and those three characters mean something like "things heard and noted."
The common English translation for this work is "a record of things heard."
What it is is informal talks that Dogen gave at his first Japanese monastery called Koshoji, which was a little bit outside of Kyoto.
That area is like a suburb of Kyoto, I understand.
That temple since has burned down and is long gone; they built the new version somewhere else, which is kind of a Japanese thing to do.
What is interesting is that these words were not written down by Dogen himself; they are written down by his close student Eijo.
We think they were probably Eijo's notes to himself because he did not share this with anybody or try to publish it or anything like that.
It was found either at the end of his life or after he died, I cannot remember, by his students, and then they put it together and published it, which is like the solution to my problem.
I suddenly realized my problem is that I have all these essays and Dharma talks floating around on my computer, and I keep feeling like I should make a book.
So I just realized I do not have to make the book; I just have to die and make sure everyone has the password because you will not find scrolls of paper lying around my office; it is on the computer.
But anyway, I will stick around.
What is great about them, and I have had this on my shelf, I have a whole shelf of Dogen back there, maybe you do too.
So it is a useful thing calling this the Year of Dogen, which got me over to my Dogen shelf looking and saying, "Oh yeah, I want to read this."
This is a fairly recent translation.
There are four or five English translations, I think, with the first one published in the seventies.
This one, though, is by our famous friend, Shohaku Okumura.

We love all things Shohaku Okumura—a great, thoughtful Japanese scholar who has lived in America for thirty years and has a good ability to bridge these different worlds and just loves Dogen to death.
So anyway, I just want to share a few little excerpts from *Shobogenzo Sweet Monkey*.
The other two main *Shobogenzo* are just to get the big picture a little bit in your head; you will forget it again, but that is all right.

The one that is all the essays that is read on Tuesday nights is often referred to as the *Kana Shobogenzo*, referring to the Japanese syllabary languages because it was written in Japanese with lots of quotes, lots of Chinese quotes.
There is a third *Shobogenzo* called the *Shinji Shobogenzo*, and *Shinji* refers to Chinese, and that is all in Chinese.
It is actually just three hundred-something koans that Dogen collected with no commentary, all written out in the original Chinese.
So there are layers and layers, and the scholastic stuff does get kind of interesting; I will try not to go on about it too long.

In my initial readings from *Shobogenzo Sweet Monkey*, which I am so enjoying as much as one can enjoy Dogen, it is never like watching TV or something; it is always an effort, and it feels much more personal and connected.
The essays in the *Kana Shobogenzo* are really Dogen trying to make a deep dive for us and with us into the non-dual nature of reality.
So he tells things this way and that, and Reisle is working on that with us a little bit from one of his actually more accessible essays, *Genjokoan*.
Part of why that is more accessible is he wrote it as a letter, so it also has a little more of a conversational sort of feeling to it.
But these are like Dogen calling the monks together at this time and that time and having something he wants to say.
I suspect he did not write any of these talks out, but I am sure some of them he thought about it back in his room, what I want to say tonight or this morning to the monks.
Sometimes they were given at the scheduled Dharma talk time.
The other times, I guess, he would just pass the word somehow.
Maybe Adria would run around ringing a bell and they would gather in the Dharma room because Dogen, the teacher, wanted to say something.
Apparently, some of these were in the middle of the night too, waking them all up and saying, "This is what I want to say," telling them a story, a bedtime story.
So I noticed a couple of themes here; I want to touch on four of them.
There are more.
The text itself does not have chapter titles or headers or anything like that, like traditional texts usually do not.
It is just, "This one day Dogen said this, next day Dogen said that."
Shohaku has done a little bit of organizing, so that helped me a lot.

In his introduction, there is kind of a key: if you are interested in this theme, look at these seventeen different ones scattered around the book; if you are interested in that theme, look at these ten different little excerpts scattered around the book.
So the first thing I want to talk about is aspiration.
Aspiration is something we think about; I think, "Why am I doing this?
What inspires me?"
But it is not too central for us usually, and I think for Dogen, it was much more central than it tends to be in our mind: the sense of aspiration, inspiration, vision, direction.
We tend to think, "Am I doing it right?"
I do not think Dogen did not really think about it that way.
He did not really think about, "Am I doing it right?"
He thought about, "What is the feeling?
Why am I doing this?"
So here is a little thing on aspiration.
This is chapter three, note eleven.
There are two different main versions of the *Jui Monki*, so even that does not necessarily help you because you could get into a different translation than the other one.
Anyway, Dogen says, "One day a student asked, although I have been spending months and years aspiring to learn the way, I have not yet had any realization.
Many of the ancient masters said that the Buddha way does not depend on intelligence, nor require wide knowledge or sharp-wittedness.
Therefore, I do not think I should disparage myself because I do not get it.
I should not disparage myself for my inferior capacity and lack of wisdom.
Is there something about this that has been handed down in tradition that I should keep in mind?"
That is how this one starts.
A student makes a statement and asks Dogen a question.
Ajo is there, jotting this down.
So this is kind of interesting; the student has confidence, some, right?
I am going to say he, because probably, it was a man.
Confidence he is on the right track because he has heard the teachings that this does not depend on special knowledge or intelligence.
Dogen says that a lot, right?
But still he is not totally confident; he has to ask after saying, "Ah, it is okay that I get it, that it is okay, I do not get it."
Then he has to ask at the end, "But is there something else?
Is there something handed down that would help me?"
So that is often where we are.
We are starting to have a little confidence over time.
"It is okay.
I am okay the way I am, right?
Perfect just as I am."
And yeah, there is some improvement needed.
So Dogen answers in Ajo's notes: "Dogen instructed, You are right.
Attaining the way does not require intelligence or talent, nor does it depend on quick-wittedness.
Nonetheless, in the genuine study of the way, it is a mistake to encourage a student to be like a blind, deaf, or ignorant person.
Because having a wide knowledge or great talent is not required, we should not disparage ourselves because of our inferior capacity.
True practice of the way should be easy."
So that is kind of interesting; I will read that again.
Yes, "You are right.
Attaining the way does not require special intelligence or talent or quick-wittedness.
But nonetheless, we should not be like a blind, deaf, or ignorant person.
We should still pay attention.
We should still learn.
We should still study."
So it is a both-and deal, right?
And because having a wide knowledge or great talent is not required, we should not disparage ourselves because of our inferior capacity, and true practice of the way should be easy.
Easy is not the first thing you think of when you hear about Dogen teachings.
However, a couple of sections later, he also talks about that it also can be hard.
I heard something a little bit later: "Although some people depart from their homes and give up family or property, there are those who have not yet given up their bodies.
They think they should not do anything physically painful and avoid practicing anything that might cause sickness, even though they know this too is the Buddha way.
So we also should practice until our bodies just, you know, we temper this a little now, but there is something to being, you know, serious, right?
So it should be easy, but we also may need to tolerate difficulty, you know, and physical difficulty, right?"
Another question is, I just had somebody in Doko's own room saying, "How do I deal with all this pain in my hips and knees?"
And of course, we want to be more comfortable if we can be.
But will we ever be completely comfortable?
No, no.
So easy and not easy.
Also, like the other thing I like about this is that, like all Dharma teachers, Dogen's teachings were responsive to who he was talking to, probably, right?
It is about both sides, easy and hard, hard and easy.
And also the mistake of thinking about easy and hard, right?
And that we need, we need all of it, you know?
But here, yeah, again, it is not about skill; it is about aspiration.
It is about confidence.
It is about showing up.
There is a sense of ease here, which maybe helps us through the difficulty.
This causes me to encourage us all, myself included, to reflect more often on aspiration: "Why am I doing this?
What am I bringing to practice?
And am I slipping into thinking, 'How do I do this right?
I am no good at it?
You know, I need to learn more stuff?
Maybe projecting onto others, you know, 'Oh, they are good at it.
I am not good at it,' which is not this, right?
That is a mistake.
It is not about that; it is about our hearts.
It is about our intention.
It is about our love for the Dharma."
Another time, Dogen praised as one of Buddha's early students, another section of *Sui Mokki*, who was not really good at remembering anything.
Here is that section, Dogen speaking: "While the Tathagata was in the world, there was a monk whose name was Kuddha Pontika.
And it was difficult for him to remember and recite even a single verse.
But because his aspiration was so earnest and strong, he attained verification within one summer practice period."

So I think this is an important thing to think about, that we of course are going to default to our cultural norm, which is skill, talent, knowledge, steps, looking good, looking like we are doing it right, not embarrassing ourselves, rejection on others that are better than me or they are worse than me, which is kind of the same thing.
But Dogen says, "No, no, no.
It is about your aspiration.
It is not about that."
So that is the first thing that I have noticed in *Sui Mokki*: an emphasis on aspiration to aspire.
Second thing that is in here very strongly are teachings on impermanence.
This is surely connected to our attitude around practice: impermanence, change, fluidity, emptiness.
I really recognize that our minds, our conventional mind, does feel threatened by impermanence, which means that we feel threatened by the fundamental way that everything actually is.
So this is a big problem; this is the root of deep issues and suffering.
I was actually reading an interview this morning in the New York Times with a neuroscientist while I was goofing off before I sat down to finish my talk.
I saw this article, and the neuroscientist was talking about memory.

He is saying that the main purpose of memory is to kind of ward off impermanence; that we remember and we regenerate memories, and we are not really remembering things exactly the way they happen, to create a sense of stability and order and a sense-making about who we are because we remember all the things that happened in our lives, and our life has a sensible story to it, and who we are has some consistency in our retold stories of ourselves.
I am that kind of a person.
I responded that way the other time.
The neuroscientist must have been saying, "Well, actually, everything is changing, including our memories.
Every time we bring them up, we retell them in a different way in psychology."
So that is interesting, huh?
So there is a way that our whole life is kind of warding off something that is ever-present.
And so Dharma is a deep process of accepting and healing and opening to impermanence.
And then how we relate to impermanence is like probably the core ingredient in freedom and in suffering, freedom from suffering, suffering and freedom from suffering.
So here is Dogen.
Here is one of the ways he brought it up: "Once we have aroused our aspiration, so C connects to this, once we have aroused our aspiration, we should think solely of the impermanence of the world.
This is not a matter of fusing some method.
This is not a matter of using some method of meditative contemplation, understanding permanence."
It's not a matter of fabricating something in our minds that does not exist; no, impermanence is truly the reality right in front of our eyes.
We need not wait for some teaching from others, some proof, some passage of scripture or some principle.
Born in the morning and dead in the evening, the person we saw yesterday is no longer here today.
This is what we see with our eyes, heart, and ears.

During our lifetime, that we may experience pleasure, sorrow, and love from our families and hatred for our enemies, if we can untie the entanglements of our thinking, we can spend our lives without being bothered by any such thing.
We simply think of the Buddha way and seek joy for all living beings.
For aged people whose lives are already half over, see any of those around here?
For aged people whose lives are already more than half over, this is true all the more.
How many years remain?
How can we slacken in our study of the way?
That's great.
Isn't this interesting?
It feels really like a person talking to us so directly.
It's a different voice, isn't it, than the regular Kana Shobogen.
By now he'd be telling us there is no time and there is no life and death; we'd be all confused.
It's also a younger Dogen.
He was in his late thirties, early forties when these talks were given.

The Koshoji monastery where these were given, although it was a full-on monastery, it had a monks' hall where the monks lived and practiced, one of the first monks' halls in Japan, but it was more on the edge of town.
I think people came and went a lot more; there were visitors and laypeople there a lot.
So we don't totally know anything really about Dogen, but about his life or his inner motivations.
We just have all these writings, that's my theory.
He was younger in his career; he was just being more colloquial and direct.
He was talking to an audience, newer to practice and more diverse audience as well.
Later at Ehiji, he was talking to the monks in a remote place where nobody's coming and going, so he just went for the deep dharma there.
It's good to have both; we need both, the accessible dharma and the deep dharma.
But anyway, it's not a teaching, it's not a meditation; it's right in front of your nose, and your heart, the heart is mentioned here.
And although we may experience pleasure, sorrow, and pain, as we learn to not be bothered by this, not upset by impermanence, fully accept impermanence, we're okay.
This is such a hopeful message: we're okay.
We just rest in the Buddha way; we seek joy for all living beings.
And we don't know how long we have, and that's okay.
So keep practicing.
This, of course, makes me probably, too, think about important transitions and the big changes, right?
Change is happening all the time, but it comes to mind more clearly when there's a big transition like a death or a marriage or a birth, the big things, a big graduation.
Wow, I've got a whole new life now.
We had a whole new life yesterday, too, right?
And one came up for me.
It wasn't one I experienced directly, rather indirectly.
I was thinking this morning of Norman's long, long-time friend and Dharma companion, a fellow named Alan Liu.
Now, Norman and Alan met, I think, in college and came out to California.
I think not together, but one after the other.
They both came to California in 1970, Hippie Dharma, California.
They trained together at Berkeley's Zen Center.
Alan was also Jewish, and he ended up making the Jewish part of his identity his primary practice, and Buddhism and Zen as the support, whereas Norman went the other way.
But they stayed close.
Alan went on to become a rabbi.
Norman, of course, ends up becoming a Zen priest and an abbot of San Francisco's Zen Center.
And through it all, they found ways to stay connected and collaborate.
They created a Jewish meditation center together in San Francisco called Makoror, and just, I think, loved each other to death, you know, and appreciated each other about the same age.
I remember one time we were on retreat with Norman.
It was either in Vancouver or this camp outside Vancouver.
I can't remember when it was, early eighties, maybe.
I guess I could look on Alan's Wikipedia page and find out.
Anyway, while on retreat with us, Norman gets the word that Alan went out on a jog one morning, that morning, and was found dead by the side of the road, probably a brain aneurysm.
And being at retreat and giving us talks, Norman was very open about how he was processing this and working with it and being with it.
I think he kind of couldn't help but share, actually.
It was big, like the biggest blow you could imagine.
Shook him to his core.
And there's a lot of things I could say about that.
But the thing I remember most strongly was what came up for him was aspiration, back to Dogen's first theme.
So aspiration and impermanence come together.

Norman shared with us a strong aspiration to be more compassionate, and shared with us he felt like he was not compassionate enough, you know, a little too focused on his own concerns, you know, a little too willing to hole up in his studio and read lots of poetry books and not be bothered by anybody.
And that Alan had been an example for him, to him, of someone who was really out there and really in compassion and love for all beings all the time.
And he felt like in Alan's memory he should become more compassionate.
And of course, being Norman's devoted students, we're like, no, no, no, you're compassionate, you're compassionate.
People reassure me like that too sometimes now.
It's kind of cute, you know?
It's like, no, no, no, that's not the point.
That's something I'm actually working on.
This is real for me, you know?
But it was so touching to me, you know, that that's where he went with it, you know, and sad too.
And I'm sure angry and upset too, although he didn't say that out loud, you know, why should this happen, you know?
But maybe aspiration and impermanence go together in such deep, deep ways if we're open to them, you know, or in practice, of course, helps so much.
And, of course, lots of other, you know, transitions and deep impermanences are floating around the song of life right now.
We just cremated one member and had a memorial for him that was quite lovely from Michael Kalbarer.
And a couple of days ago, I was visiting with Edie Norton, who is now on hospice.
She's doing okay.
There's not an eminent thing that's going to, you know, do her in.
Besides, she has a serious heart condition, but seems to be okay.
But she's on hospice.
She's towards the end, you know.
She's acknowledging that and accepting that.
She's on oxygen all the time.
She doesn't really go out anymore because it's increasingly hard and a big project to go out anywhere.
Her son comes over.
Dharma friends come over.
Many people come over.
Hospice people come over.
Limited inner energy, a little frustrated by it, you know, but accepting it, you know.
Her mind is just sharp as ever.
It's definitely Edie, you know.
She told me all kinds of things, you know.
And just being as conscious as she can be in the process of aging and dying.
But one of the reasons I was there actually was so poignant, you know, and it's always true, but it was so clear this time.
We're actually preparing ahead for the Jukai that we'll have in November.
A ways off, right?
But not too far.
Edie and I were working on picking someone's name together, someone who's close to Edie.
And we did this fully expecting that Edie would not be alive in November.
Maybe she will be.
That would be a wonderful surprise.
But that was our expectation as we did this, you know.
What a thing, you know.
And it didn't actually feel sad.
It felt real, you know.
It felt deep.
It felt important.
And it felt like a helpful truth for me to feel into for all the time, you know.
Whenever we're talking to somebody about something next November, we don't know, right?
We don't know.
So aspiration and impermanence.
So it's another important thing to look at: how do you meet impermanence, you know?
Since our brain is so often busy avoiding impermanence, we have to kind of, you know, catch ourselves out sometimes, you know.
Oh, look at that.
Denying the nature of change, you know, like when we're upset when something breaks, you know, as if that wasn't the nature of everything to break, you know.
Nobody's perfect at this.
I'm still mad at our little milk foamer in the kitchen.
Great little machine.
Like you put the milk in and you push the button, it makes this wonderful foamy milk, you know.
And of course, we bought the cheap one from China because that's what's on Amazon.
And it died six months later.
We haven't decided whether to replace it, so it's sitting there.
So it's a little impermanence thing for me every time I go in there.
And a little anger shows up, you know, because that's my resistance to impermanence.
Like, dang it, they should have made this better, you know.
So that's just a little thing to remind me that it's a big thing, impermanence.
Two more themes and then I'm excited to have a little conversation.

The third theme I noticed here is generosity, and a kind of a true generosity, and it connects to something we hear in Suzuki Roshi all the time, which is to have no gaining idea with your generous activity.
And the practice itself is not something to get something up; it's an act of generosity.
So the famous dana paramita, right, the perfection of giving.
There's one, there's as many passages about this, and the one I like the best is, he starts out talking about examples from lay life, and then he pivots into monastic life.
So again, I think where he was and the time he was, he was kind of talking to lay people and monastics together.
Here's Dogen from Ejo's memory, written down almost a thousand years ago.
Isn't this wild, you know?
It's like you're in the room.
*Dogen.
Among the laity, I see the people who have had good fortune and have enabled their families to prosper are all honest and work for the benefit of others.
This means that they maintain their family prosperity and their descendants will not die out in later generations.*
This is something he's noticed, he says.
Among the laity, I see that people who have good fortune have enabled their families to prosper are honest and work for the benefit of others.
This means they maintain their family prosperity and their descendants do not die out in later generations.
But those who are dishonest or who harm others may seem to temporarily receive good fortune and be able to maintain their livelihood for a while, but in the end, their prosperity will decline.
Even if such people seem to spend their lifetime without trouble, their descendants will know great misfortune.
So this is karma, right?

Further, when we do good things for others, if we do so because of our desire to be well thought of or to ingratiate ourselves with others, even though this is better than doing harmful things, such actions do not truly benefit others because we're only thinking of the benefit to ourselves.

But if we do beneficial things for others with humility, even if they do not notice the benefit, or we do beneficial things for future generations without considering benefit for ourselves, then we are truly doing good things for others.
So it's about humility, right?
It's about the intention.
So aspiration is here too, right?
In our generosity.
So he brings up these examples from lay life, and then he talks to the monks for a while about how this looks in the monastery.
I'll skip that part.
And then he kind of brings it all together.
The ancient way of practicing in this way, generously, is to renounce the world and cast aside the self.
The ancient way for practicing in this way is to renounce the world and cast aside the self, only if we have truly thrown away the self, when we have no desire to be well thought of by others.
However, if we think, I don't care what others may think, and act unwholesomely or self-indulgently, we go against the will of the Buddha.
So here he's talking about selflessness, but warning us not to misunderstand selflessness, right?
So free from self, giving generously, and that doesn't mean, yeah, I don't care what they think of me, right?
I don't care what they think about you, but not that kind of attitude.
So that's a really old attitude, I guess, you know?
Ancient, you know?
I don't care what you think.
Warned the monks about that so long ago.
So it's a certain kind of selflessness.
He goes on.
You should not think about gaining anything in return for your good reputation.
You should do things knowing there is nothing to be gained and work for the sake of benefiting others.
This is the primary point to bear in mind in order to achieve release from our ego clinging.
To maintain this mind is not desiring gain.
We must first of all be mindful of impermanence.
One's lifetime is like a dream.
Time passes swiftly.
Our do-like lives will disappear before the dawn.
While we are alive for this short time, we must resolve to perform beneficial actions for others and follow the will of the Buddha and not do it for our own self-gain.
So now you can see all three of these themes being woven together, right?
It's about aspiration, it's about impermanence, and it's about selfless generosity.
That's the path he's describing to us.
And again, what I think I'll be studying the rest of my life is that it's not about skill.
We get so focused on this, right?
We have meetings and agendas and plans and schedules.
and do this or we do that, we do it this way, do it that way, and that all matters.
But maybe not in the way we think it does.
The secret ingredient is not that we did it just right or the retreat was just the right length or the ceremony was just right or you said just the right thing in that email.
Maybe that wasn't why it went well or didn't go well.
Maybe it's more about these three factors: aspiration, being in touch with impermanence, and selfless generosity.

And that brings up something from my own life, and I don't want to make this too much about me, but it was kind of coming out for me, so I'll share a little bit, and maybe you can reflect on how this has worked in your life as well.

Which is I've actually really, you know, I mean, it's been enough years now, you think I could stop repeating this story, but it's such a part of my story, which is a kind of struggle with livelihood.
On the one hand, I'm privileged and college-educated, and I kind of, you know, I had so many choices, right?
I could come to everything, so it's not like a big problem.
I had it good.
But I had trouble figuring out what to do.

I worked in five different professions maybe, you know, to a certain level, you know, and did professional trainings, and none of them quite worked out, you know, and I just felt like I was stumbling around and trying to figure it out, and I couldn't figure it out, and I just couldn't find what my true aspiration was.
And then, in the course of all that, I ran into Zen practice.
You could feel at some deep, I don't know, intuitive level, I didn't really have words for it.
This was really important.
I didn't necessarily even like it that much, you know what I mean?
I don't know how much I really like Zazen, you know what I mean?
It's not like, oh boy, I can't wait, you know?
But I could feel its importance, you know?

And so coming to Bellingham, I knew that I wouldn't really be able to keep it up unless I had support, and the places I'd learned it, there were lots of people around, like lots of support, that was my model, you know?
So I didn't think I could create a new Green Gulch or a new Santa Cruz Zen Center, although it seems like we are doing the second thing there.
But I figured, well, I could find a few friends maybe, and Norman encouraged me to do that.
I went to him one time, and I went to him one time and said, "Yeah, yeah, I'm giving it up, I don't think I can keep this up."
And he said, "No, no, no, I think you can keep it up.
Find some friends."
So anyway, I did.
You know, I put a note up at Village Books before there was no internet, you know?
And rented a room, you know, first in our living room, and then rented a little room at the library, and people came kind of right away, you know?
And little by little it grew, as you know, and here we are today, in all the different ways that this has happened, you know?
Owning a building and thinking about doing a major expense of remodel, like what?
You know, how's this even possible?
And over those years, I made many choices, right?
You know, and many discussions with others, and many other people participated in those many choices, and some were skillful, some were not so skillful.
I have some scars in my heart of people who left the sangha because I didn't understand them or said something wrong or don't even understand why, you know?
Just bad fit, you know?
Personalities are personalities.
So I'm not like I ever got perfect at any of this, but somehow, in some intuitive way, some aspiration awoke in me early that I don't know if I'll ever understand.

While I was putting all my busy energy and trying to figure out whether to be a biologist or an elementary school teacher or a carpenter, you know, I was, without thinking about it quite as much, just taking care of the sitting group every week and going every week, and I don't even know why did I go every week?
It just seemed like the thing to do.
